title: Rotated vs Axis-Parallel: The Last Barrier
content: After BKU (2024) solved the axis-parallel case of Erdős #106, the remaining question is whether allowing rotation gives strictly better packings. This file formalizes the infrastructure to state and reason about this question.
mathContext: The axis-parallel problem: pack n unit squares in [0,1]² with sides parallel to the axes, maximize total side-length. BKU proved g(k²+1) = k. The rotated problem: same but squares may be rotated. f_rot(n) ≥ g(n) trivially; the question is whether strict inequality holds.

title: RotatedSquare: Parametrized by Center, Side, Angle
content: The RotatedSquare structure captures a square by its center, side length, and rotation angle. The interior is defined by rotating the test point back to the axis-parallel frame: p is inside iff rotating (p - center) by -θ lands in (-s/2, s/2)².
mathContext: RotatedSquare: center $(c_x, c_y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, side $s > 0$, angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$. Interior: $\{p \mid |r_x| < s/2 \wedge |r_y| < s/2\}$ where $(r_x, r_y) = R_{-\theta}(p - c)$ and $R_{-\theta}$ is rotation by $-\theta$.

title: Interior via Inverse Rotation: Coordinate Formula
content: The interior formula rotates the displacement vector (dx, dy) = p - center by angle -θ via the 2×2 matrix: rx = dx·cos θ + dy·sin θ, ry = -dx·sin θ + dy·cos θ. These are the standard rotation-matrix components for angle -θ, verifiable by noting cos(-θ) = cos θ and sin(-θ) = -sin θ.
mathContext: $r_x = \Delta x \cos\theta + \Delta y \sin\theta$, $r_y = -\Delta x \sin\theta + \Delta y \cos\theta$. This is rotation by $-\theta$: the point is in the interior iff $|r_x| < s/2$ and $|r_y| < s/2$, i.e., it lies in the $(-s/2, s/2)^2$ axis-aligned box.

title: GeneralPacking and g(n)/f_rot(n) as Suprema
content: GeneralPacking is a Fin n-indexed family with containment (closure ⊆ [0,1]²) and pairwise disjoint interiors. AxisParallelPacking extends it with angle=0. The objective functions f_rot and g_ap are defined as suprema of achievable sum-sets — this is the standard real-analysis approach when explicit maxima may not be attained.
mathContext: $f_{\text{rot}}(n) = \sup\{\sum_i s_i \mid (S_i) \text{ is a GeneralPacking}\}$, $g(n) = \sup$ over AxisParallelPacking. The supremum is used rather than maximum since it's unclear whether the sup is attained (compactness arguments would be needed).

title: Axis-Parallel ⊆ General: Trivial Direction via rfl
content: achievable_sums_subset proves that every axis-parallel packing is a general packing, so all achievable AP sums are also achievable as general sums. This immediately gives g(n) ≤ f_rot(n) via csSup monotonicity (proved in g_ap_le_f_rot at line 378). The proof is trivially one line: P.toGeneralPacking inherits from AxisParallelPacking extends GeneralPacking.
mathContext: $\{s \mid \exists P : \text{AP}(n), P.\text{sum} = s\} \subseteq \{s \mid \exists P : \text{Gen}(n), P.\text{sum} = s\}$. Combined with $\text{sSup}$ monotonicity, this gives $g(n) \leq f_{\text{rot}}(n)$. The actual inequality is in theorem g_ap_le_f_rot (line 378) using csSup_le_csSup.

title: side ≤ √2: Key Geometric Bound via Edge Midpoints
content: side_le_sqrt_two proves that any square contained in [0,1]² has side ≤ √2 (regardless of rotation). The proof uses the four edge midpoints: if the square is in [0,1]², then s|cos θ| ≤ 1 and s|sin θ| ≤ 1 (since opposite edge midpoints are in [0,1]² and their difference has magnitude s|cos θ|). Then s² = s²(cos²θ + sin²θ) ≤ 2.
mathContext: Opposite edge midpoints: $c \pm (s/2)(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. Both in $[0,1]^2$ forces $s|\cos\theta| \leq 1$ (from x-coordinates). Similarly $s|\sin\theta| \leq 1$. Then $s^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = s^2 \leq (s\cos\theta)^2 + (s\sin\theta)^2 \leq 2$.

title: The Open Question: rotationHelps vs rotationNeverHelps
content: rotationHelps := ∃ n, f_rot n > g_ap n (rotation strictly improves). rotationNeverHelps := ∀ n, f_rot n = g_ap n (rotation never helps). These are logically complementary (by excluded middle and the fact that g_ap ≤ f_rot). The Erdős problem is to determine which holds — no example of rotationHelps is known.
mathContext: We have $g(n) \leq f_{\text{rot}}(n)$ always (proved). rotationNeverHelps would mean equality everywhere. Since $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2) = g(k^2) = k$ at perfect squares, any rotation advantage must occur at non-perfect-square n, with n=k²+1 being the most interesting case.

title: BKU Bridge: rotationNeverHelps + BKU → Full Erdős Conjecture
content: bku_and_no_rotation_implies_general proves: if rotation never helps (f_rot = g globally), then the full Erdős conjecture f_rot(k²+1) = k follows from the BKU axis-parallel result g(k²+1) = k. The proof is one rewrite: rw [h] converts the f_rot question to a g question, then bku_theorem_ap closes it.
mathContext: Chain: rotationNeverHelps $\Rightarrow$ $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) = g(k^2+1) = k$ (BKU). This is the key decomposition: the general problem separates into a geometric part (does rotation help?) and a combinatorial part (axis-parallel packing). BKU resolved the combinatorial part; the geometric part remains open.
